title: TAC-CoT: Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens

paper.title: TAC-CoT : Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
paper.abstract: Abstract LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8 × 6.8\times . Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: To enhance the problem-solving ability of large language models (LLMs), a wide range of reasoning-oriented methods have been explored. In particular, for tasks that require accurate and reliable reasoning, such as mathematical reasoning and knowledge-intensive question answering, research has evolved toward Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which improves models’ internal reasoning capabilities through intermediate reasoning steps Wei et al. (2022) ; DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025b) , as well as agentic tool-use frameworks, which enhance rigor and factuality by enabling models to interact with external tools during problem solving Zhang et al. (2026) ; Kim et al. (2026) . Figure 2: Overview of TAC-CoT compared with the Explicit-CoT agent and implicit-CoT methods. TAC-CoT uses implicit CoT as its reasoning backbone while preserving interaction segments in explicit natural language. This design enables implicit CoT to use tools and allocate query-dependent implicit reasoning budgets, improving efficiency, performance, and robustness over the Explicit-CoT agent. Here, n n denotes the number of discrete tokens generated by the Explicit-CoT agent at each step, b b denotes the number of continuous tokens in each implicit reasoning segment of TAC-CoT , and m m denotes the fixed continuous-token budget used by prior implicit-CoT methods. Most prior work adopts the explicit CoT paradigm, where intermediate reasoning is represented as human-readable natural-language tokens. This paradigm is attractive because it is directly compatible with autoregressive generation and provides an interpretable interface between reasoning and action Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) . However, verbalizing the entire reasoning process substantially increases inference cost as reasoning traces grow longer and makes the model more susceptible to error accumulation across intermediate steps Han et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2026) . Implicit CoT has emerged as an alternative paradigm that replaces readable natural-language rationales with compact continuous thought tokens . By performing reasoning in non-verbal latent spaces, implicit CoT aims to retain the benefits of multi-step reasoning while mitigating the inference cost and vulnerability to error accumulation of lengthy textual traces Shen et al. (2025) . Despite these benefits, implicit CoT methods are ill-suited for LLM-based agent systems. They rely on a fixed number of implicit tokens to carry the entire reasoning process of every query, which gives rise to two limitations. First, since the implicit-token budget is consumed in a single uninterrupted block before the final answer Deng et al. (2024) ; Wei et al. (2026) , there is no intermediate point at which the model can emit an explicit tool call or ingest an observation, so tool use is structurally infeasible. Second, the same token count is applied to every input regardless of its difficulty or the number of intermediate decision points it requires Wu et al. (2026) ; Aggarwal et al. (2026) . As a result, prior implicit CoT methods cannot interact with external environments and under-allocate reasoning capacity to more difficult queries. In this paper, we propose TAC-CoT ( T ool-empowered A daptive C ontinuous CoT), which interleaves compact implicit reasoning segments with explicit tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers . Rather than carrying the entire reasoning process in a single block of implicit tokens, TAC-CoT reasons within a short implicit segment and then either invokes a tool or produces the answer, resuming with another segment after each tool observation. This interleaving simultaneously addresses both limitations of prior implicit CoT, as explicit tokens between segments make tool use executable, while the number of segments, determined on the fly, makes the reasoning budget query-adaptive. To train this behavior, we automatically construct tool-use trajectories from reasoning datasets and supervise the model to perform compact latent reasoning between tool invocations. Our contributions are summarized as follows. (1) We extend implicit CoT to tool-empowered agentic systems, enabling compact continuous reasoning in iterative reasoning–action workflows. (2) We show that TAC-CoT improves reasoning performance while substantially reducing the number of reasoning tokens compared with explicit CoT-style reasoning by interleaving continuous thought tokens with explicit tokens. (3) We introduce an adaptive token-allocation mechanism that flexibly adjusts the length of implicit reasoning according to query difficulty. (4) As highlighted in Figure 1 , TAC-CoT improves downstream task performance while using the forward reasoning budget more efficiently. Our analysis shows that TAC-CoT benefits from query-adaptive implicit reasoning budgets, improves tool-using scenarios, and mitigates error accumulation through implicit reasoning.

sections.heading: 2 TAC-CoT : Tool-Empowered Implicit CoT via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
sections.text: We explain TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered implicit CoT framework that interleaves latent reasoning segments with explicit, executable tool interactions. We first describe TAC-CoT ’s inference procedure (§ 2.1 ), then how we construct training trajectories (§ 2.2 ), and finally the learning objective (§ 2.3 ). Algorithm 1 shows its inference procedure.

sections.heading: Deciding When to Call a Tool.
sections.text: A key design decision of TAC-CoT is when to interrupt latent reasoning for an external interaction. At the end of every implicit segment C ( i ) C^{(i)} , TAC-CoT compares the logits of the tool call u ( i ) u^{(i)} and answer options to decide the next step. If the tool-call logit is higher, TAC-CoT emits a tool call, appends the returned observation o ( i ) o^{(i)} to the context, and starts another implicit segment. Otherwise, the current segment becomes the consolidating segment C ( k ) C^{(k)} , from which the final answer is generated. Unlike prior implicit CoT methods that consume a fixed implicit budget before any explicit output, this per-segment routing is what makes tool use feasible under implicit reasoning.

sections.heading: Query-Adaptive Continuous-Thought Token Budget.
sections.text: Since the tool call decision is made after every implicit segment, the total reasoning budget becomes query-adaptive . Simple queries may terminate after a single segment, while more complex queries can continue through multiple tool interactions. Thus, b b is fixed only locally within each segment. In contrast, if TAC-CoT terminates after k k implicit segments C ( i ) C^{(i)} , it uses k ​ b kb continuous tokens in total, where k k is determined dynamically during inference.

sections.heading: 2.2 Dataset Construction for Agentic CoT
sections.text: Realizing our interleaved inference mechanism in Eq ( 2 ) requires training data that exposes the explicit counterpart τ E \tau_{E} of the interleaved trajectory τ I \tau_{I} . That is, each example must provide the full sequence of explicit reasoning segments ℛ ( i ) \mathcal{R}^{(i)} , tool calls u ( i ) u^{(i)} , observations o ( i ) o^{(i)} , and the final answer a a , from which TAC-CoT learns to replace each ℛ ( i ) \mathcal{R}^{(i)} with an implicit segment C ( i ) C^{(i)} while preserving the surrounding explicit interactions. We construct such data with two strategies depending on whether the source dataset already includes executable tool interactions, or only reasoning traces and gold answers. • Sources with Tool Interactions. We convert the provided executable annotations into tool calls. If the executable annotations are provided separately from the reasoning traces, we match their tool-call parameters and returned observations to the corresponding reasoning spans. We then normalize the matched interactions into a unified tool-call format with explicit tool names and parameters, and insert the tool calls and observations into the reasoning trajectory. • Sources without Tool Interactions. As intermediate interactions are not directly available, we instead employ a stronger LLM (DeepSeek-V3; See Appendix A ) as a tool-augmented solver to synthesize them. Given a question and the available tools, the model generates a complete trajectory with interleaved reasoning spans, tool calls, observations, and a predicted answer. We retain only trajectories whose predicted answers match the source gold answers, and normalize the retained trajectories into the same format. Figure 3: Training objective of TAC-CoT . The student generates continuous thought tokens, from which explicit reasoning chunks are reconstructed for supervision. Explicit outputs are trained with cross-entropy loss, while answer-boundary hidden states are distilled from an explicit-CoT teacher. The final objective combines student, teacher, and distillation losses.

sections.heading: 3 Experiments
sections.text: We design experiments to evaluate two capabilities of our proposed method: (1) agentic math problem-solving training and evaluation to assess its reasoning capability, and (2) agentic QA training and evaluation to assess its agentic capability.

sections.heading: Training Datasets.
sections.text: TAC-CoT requires training to use implicit tokens. To evaluate mathematical reasoning, we use GSM8K-Aug-NL ( Deng et al., 2024 ) , which contains explicit interactions as textual explanations. Since GSM8K-Aug-NL contains explicit reasoning trajectories without executable interfaces, we insert executable calculator annotations from GSM8K-Aug ( Deng et al., 2024 ) . To evaluate QA capability, we use the HotpotQA Yang et al. (2018) dataset. We construct 40,000 trajectories by using DeepSeek-V3 ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025a ) with the available tool and allowing it to solve each question through iterative tool interaction. We retain only trajectories whose final answer matches the gold annotation. Although teacher-generated trajectories may inherit teacher-specific biases, TAC-CoT and all QA baselines are trained on the same trajectories; such biases are therefore shared across methods and cannot by themselves explain TAC-CoT’s relative improvements. Dataset construction details are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: Evaluation Benchmarks.
sections.text: We evaluate TAC-CoT on agentic math problem solving (Math), agentic Question-Answering (QA), and tool-use benchmarks, as summarized in Table 1 . On toolBench, we use ‘Single’ for the I1 single-tool scenario, and ‘Multi’ as the I2 + I3 multi-tool scenario. We report accuracy (Acc) for math tasks and exact match (EM) for QA. To compare the inference cost independently of hardware and external API latency , we report the average number of forward passes (# Fwd) Kuzina et al. (2026) ; Wei et al. (2026) . For no-tool QA setting (TU = ✗ ), # Fwd also includes autoregressive generation of missing tool observations; see Appendix B.2 .

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , and Qwen3-4B Yang et al. (2025) as backbone models. For agentic QA, we use the Wikipedia API as the search engine, following Yao et al. (2022) . Further details are provided in Appendix B . We provide pseudocode for reproducibility in Figure 10 . For TAC-CoT , we set B = 3 B=3 . Ablation results for different B B values are provided in Appendix C.1 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare TAC-CoT against (1) an Explicit-CoT agent, which serves as a strong baseline for tool use and reasoning by using full explicit reasoning traces, fine-tuned on the same training trajectories as our method; (2) TokenSkip Xia et al. (2025) , an explicit CoT method that compresses intermediate reasoning trajectories by pruning low-importance tokens; (3) PCCoT Wu et al. (2025) , which updates implicit thought tokens in parallel using Jacobi iteration, improving efficiency over sequential implicit CoT; (4) CODI Shen et al. (2025) , an implicit-CoT method trained via trajectory-level self-distillation from CoT-based teacher signals; and (5) SIM-CoT Wei et al. (2026) , which extends CODI by adding step-level supervision to reconstruct reasoning steps from latent embeddings.

sections.heading: 3.2 Main Results
sections.text: Our evaluation examines whether TAC-CoT achieves its design goals in addressing the limitations of extending existing CoT approaches to agentic systems, focusing on four aspects: tool-use effectiveness, internal reasoning ability, query-adaptive continuous-thought budgeting, and inference efficiency. Table 2 presents the main results on agentic math and QA benchmarks across tool-calling and no-tool settings.

sections.heading: Performance on Agentic Reasoning.
sections.text: Overall, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms Explicit-CoT and the other baselines. Averaged over all backbone models, Our method improves math accuracy by 5.8%p and QA performance by 2.4 points compared with Explicit-CoT. The gains also transfer to out-of-domain benchmarks: Ours improves math performance by 6.5%p in-domain and 5.5%p out-of-domain, and QA performance by 2.4 points in-domain and 2.5 points out-of-domain. This consistent trend suggests that TAC-CoT provides robust adaptive implicit reasoning beyond the training-domain distribution. To isolate the effect of implicit reasoning from external tool execution, we compare TAC-CoT with other baselines in the no-tool setting on math datasets. While TokenSkip, which shortens rationales by pruning tokens, underperforms Explicit-CoT, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms the Explicit-CoT agent across all math datasets. These results indicate that the improvement in internal reasoning does not simply come from shorter reasoning traces. Consistently, TAC-CoT also outperforms baselines that either remove natural-language reasoning entirely or retain concise, explicit reasoning with tool use; see Appendix C.2 .

sections.heading: Effectiveness of TAC-CoT .
sections.text: The effectiveness of TAC-CoT comes from both tool-use and query-adaptive implicit reasoning. Tool-use substantially improves QA performance, yielding up to a 29.9 point average gain over the no-tool variant while reducing forward passes by 13.3 × \times on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Even without tools, TAC-CoT benefits from adaptive budgeting: on math benchmarks, its no-tool variant outperforms prior implicit-CoT baselines while requiring far fewer forward passes than explicit CoT. These results show that TAC-CoT improves efficiency and performance by adaptively allocating continuous reasoning, with additional gains when external knowledge is needed. Supplementary full fine-tuning results are provided in Appendix C.3 .

sections.heading: Error Accumulation Mitigation.
sections.text: Table 2 shows that TAC-CoT improves internal reasoning even without external execution. To test whether this comes from reduced error accumulation, we analyze reasoning compression and length mismatch. First, we progressively replace explicit reasoning segments with implicit ones when training Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on the augmented GSM8K trajectories. We vary the replacement depth from one to four segments, since four corresponds to the 90th percentile of the number of explicit reasoning segments in the training trajectories. As shown in Table 4 , average accuracy on GSM8K, GSM-Hard, and SVAMP increases monotonically as more segments become implicit, suggesting that implicit CoT mitigates errors from lengthy rationales. Second, following the step-efficiency analysis of prior work Wu et al. (2026) , we group GSM8K examples by the offset between generated and gold reasoning lengths. Figure 5 shows that both Explicit-CoT and TAC-CoT perform best under matched lengths and degrade under over-thinking offsets. However, TAC-CoT degrades less, indicating that implicit reasoning reduces the penalty from unnecessary intermediate steps. We discuss further analysis of error accumulation in Appendix C.5 . sections.heading: Query-Adaptive Continuous-Thought Budget.
sections.text: Unlike prior implicit-CoT methods that use a fixed continuous-token budget for every query, TAC-CoT adaptively allocates its total reasoning budget according to the query. This query-adaptive continuous-thought budgeting contributes to the performance gains, especially for math tasks that depend on internal reasoning. As shown in Figure 6 , the benefit becomes larger as the required number of reasoning steps increases. TAC-CoT ’s query-adaptive budgeting benefits inputs that require different amounts of internal deliberation before producing the final answer. We group GSM8K examples into five subsets according to the number of gold reasoning steps, ranging from one to five steps, and treat this number as the required reasoning depth. We then evaluate each subset separately and compare TAC-CoT without tool use against SIM-CoT, a state-of-the-art fixed-budget implicit-CoT baseline, using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Figure 6 shows that TAC-CoT consistently outperforms SIM-CoT across all reasoning-depth groups, with larger gains on examples that require more reasoning steps. The improvement increases from 4.6 points on one-step examples to 30.3 points on four-step examples. This trend suggests that assigning the same continuous-thought-token budget to every input becomes increasingly restrictive as the required number of reasoning steps grows. In contrast, TAC-CoT increases the total continuous-token budget by continuing through additional implicit reasoning segments when more reasoning steps are needed. These results demonstrate that TAC-CoT flexibly allocates reasoning budget across queries, which is especially important for reasoning-intensive tasks.

sections.heading: Inference Efficiency.
sections.text: TAC-CoT substantially reduces inference cost relative to Explicit-CoT while improving task accuracy. Across backbones, it reduces the per-query forward count by up to 2.6 × 2.6\times on math benchmarks and 6.8 × 6.8\times on QA benchmarks, with larger savings on QA due to longer multi-step trajectories. This suggests that TAC-CoT becomes increasingly beneficial for longer trajectories. Although fixed-budget implicit-CoT baselines use fewer forward passes, they do not adapt to query complexity or retrieve missing observations. This limitation is especially harmful for QA, where answers often depend on retrieved evidence, leading to pronounced performance degradation. In contrast, TAC-CoT achieves a better cost–performance trade-off by reducing inference cost relative to Explicit-CoT while avoiding the QA degradation of fixed-budget implicit-CoT methods. On a single NVIDIA L40S GPU, TAC-CoT achieves measured wall-clock speedups of 2.3× on math and 2.4× on QA. Since realized latency depends on hardware, implementation, and external API overhead, #Fwd reductions should not be interpreted directly as wall-clock speedups; see Appendix C.6 for full results.

sections.heading: Explicit and Implicit CoT.
sections.text: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves the reasoning ability of large language models by generating intermediate reasoning before the final answer Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) . CoT methods are commonly categorized as explicit or implicit, depending on whether intermediate reasoning is represented as discrete tokens or continuous representations. Explicit CoT is readable and easy to supervise Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) , but decoding long reasoning traces increases inference cost Han et al. (2025) ; Xia et al. (2025) and exacerbates stepwise error accumulation Wu et al. (2026) . Implicit CoT instead performs intermediate reasoning in continuous latent space Hao et al. (2025) ; Shen et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Wei et al. (2026) ; Kuzina et al. (2026) . For example, Coconut feeds hidden states back as continuous thought tokens Hao et al. (2025) , CODI distills explicit CoT into continuous representations Shen et al. (2025) , PCCoT updates latent thought tokens in parallel for efficient inference Wu et al. (2025) , and SIM-CoT stabilizes implicit reasoning via step-level reconstruction Wei et al. (2026) . Although these methods reduce the cost of verbalized reasoning, they are mainly designed for standalone reasoning: they typically allocate a fixed number of continuous thought tokens per query and do not expose intermediate decisions as executable interfaces, limiting their suitability for agentic settings that require repeated reasoning and acting. In contrast, TAC-CoT extends implicit CoT to tool-using agentic systems by interleaving compact latent reasoning segments with explicit tool interactions, enabling tool calling and query-adaptive reasoning budgets. At the same time, compared with explicit-CoT agents, TAC-CoT avoids the need to verbalize intermediate reasoning, thereby reducing inference cost and mitigating error accumulation from lengthy reasoning traces.

sections.heading: Tool-Using LLM Agents.
sections.text: LLMs are increasingly studied as agents that solve tasks through interleaved reasoning, tool calls, and observations Yao et al. (2022) ; Schick et al. (2023) ; Shinn et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . ReAct formalizes this reasoning–acting loop Yao et al. (2022) , while Toolformer Schick et al. (2023) and ART Paranjape et al. (2023) show that models can invoke external APIs and resume generation after tool execution. However, most tool-using agents still rely on explicit CoT Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) , whose repeated generation across multi-step interaction loops makes inference costly Han et al. (2025) ; Xia et al. (2025) ; Aytes et al. (2025) and vulnerable to error accumulation Wu et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We presented TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered adaptive continuous CoT framework that extends implicit reasoning to tool-using agentic problem solving. By interleaving compact continuous reasoning segments with explicit tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers, TAC-CoT preserves the executable interface required for agentic workflows while avoiding the cost of fully verbalized reasoning traces. Across agentic math and knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms Explicit-CoT agents in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, while using substantially fewer model forward passes. Further analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use decisions, performs better in multi-tool scenarios, mitigates error accumulation, and benefits from query-adaptive continuous thought-token allocation.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: This work has a few limitations: First, the adaptive routing mechanism operates at the segment level rather than the token level. Second, longer interaction horizons remain an important direction for evaluating the practical deployment of TAC-CoT .

sections.heading: Appendix A Details of Data Construction
sections.text: This section provides the details of the recipe described in Section 2.2 for each domain.

sections.heading: Math Problem Solving.
sections.text: The math domain follows the source-obtainable interaction setting described. For GSM8K, where data with explicit interactions already exist, we use GSM8K-Aug and GSM8K-Aug-NL, two GSM8K augmentations with 385k samples each Deng et al. (2024) . GSM8K-Aug retains only the arithmetic equations in each reasoning step (e.g., <<86.7*15*.01=13.005>> ), whereas GSM8K-Aug-NL contains only explicit reasoning (e.g. ...day, 86.7 x 15% = 13.005 coins... ). Because the two datasets have the same questions, we align examples by question and insert the equations from GSM8K-Aug into the corresponding natural language reasoning trajectory from GSM8K-Aug-NL.

sections.heading: Question-Answering.
sections.text: For HotpotQA, which provides only questions and their gold answers without faithful tool-use trajectories, we construct trajectories by prompting DeepSeek-V3 to solve each question with access to a retrieval tool. Following Yao et al. (2022) , we implement a Wikipedia retrieval system and use the ReAct-style few-shot demonstrations from their setup. The prompt template is shown in Figures 11 and 12 .

sections.heading: Quality Audit and Construction Cost.
sections.text: To assess the quality of the synthesized QA trajectories, we randomly sampled 200 trajectories and evaluated them using GPT-5.1, a model different from the DeepSeek-V3 teacher. The evaluator assessed whether the generated actions and final answers were logically valid, and judged 99% of the sampled trajectories to be valid. Generating the QA trajectories cost $102.73 in total, including generations discarded during answer-based filtering. The filtering pass rate was 56.24%. Because exact-match filtering may reject semantically correct answers expressed differently from the gold annotation, this procedure may underestimate the usable trajectory yield.

sections.heading: B.1 Training hyperparameters
sections.text: For the CODI loss weight, we set α CODI = 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{CODI}}=1 for TAC-CoT and α CODI = 10 \alpha_{\mathrm{CODI}}=10 for PCCoT, CODI, and SIM-CoT, following Shen et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Wei et al. (2026) . For TokenSkip, we use a 50% compression ratio during training to keep its number of forward passes comparable to that of TAC-CoT . For the larger Qwen3-4B backbone, we use B = 2 B=2 continuous tokens per segment for a practical training setup.

sections.heading: B.2 Implicit CoT Baseline Details
sections.text: For each implicit CoT baseline, we report the higher score between models trained on GSM8K-Aug-NL and GSM8K-Aug.

sections.heading: Evaluation benchmark.
sections.text: For math benchmarks, we evaluate on the full test sets. For QA benchmarks, we evaluate on 1,000 randomly sampled examples from each dataset. This follows approaches used by Yin et al. (2023) ; Kaesberg et al. (2025) ; Jang et al. (2025) . Specifically, we follow the standard sample-size estimate for population proportions: n 0 = Z 2 ⋅ p ⋅ ( 1 − p ) d 2 , n_{0}=\frac{Z^{2}\cdot p\cdot(1-p)}{d^{2}}, where Z = 1.96 Z=1.96 , p = 0.5 p=0.5 , and d = 0.05 d=0.05 , corresponding to a 95% confidence level and a 5% margin of error under the conservative maximum-variance assumption. This gives n 0 ≈ 384 n_{0}\approx 384 , so our choice of 1,000 examples per QA dataset is above the required sample size. Since EM and Answer Coverage are averaged binary outcomes over examples, 1,000 random samples yield a conservative worst-case 95% margin of error of approximately 1.96 ​ 0.25 / 1000 = 3.1 1.96\sqrt{0.25/1000}=3.1 percentage points before finite-population correction.

sections.heading: Calculator setting.
sections.text: For math tasks, we build a calculator database by extracting equations from the training trajectories. During evaluation, if an expression matches an entry in this database, we use the corresponding stored result. Otherwise, we process the expression before calculation and then execute it with the calculator. This design handles cases where expressions contain units or other non-numeric tokens that cannot be directly evaluated by a standard calculator.

sections.heading: ToolBench API details.
sections.text: For ToolBench, many of the original APIs are no longer available at inference time. Following Guo et al. (2024) , we therefore use MirrorAPI. Because TAC-CoT does not verbalize its reasoning, we explicitly note this in the GPT-5.1 judge prompt. sections.heading: No-tool evaluation protocol.
sections.text: For the no-tool setting (TU = ✗ ), we disable the external tool executor while preserving the trajectory format used by tool-using agents. When the model emits an action-like span, no environment-returned observation is injected. Instead, the model continues generation and produces the corresponding observation text by itself. Thus, the no-tool setting evaluates reasoning without externally supplied tool outputs. All generated observation tokens are counted in the inference cost, and we use the same answer extraction and evaluation metrics as in the tool-use setting.

sections.heading: C.1 Effect of Continuous-Thought Tokens
sections.text: We analyze the effect of the number of continuous thought tokens (CT) per continuous segment. We vary the CT budget over { 0 , 1 , 3 } \{0,1,3\} and evaluate Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct on GSM8K, GSM-Hard, and SVAMP. Table 6 shows the results. Compared to the 0 CT setting, using CT tokens improves the average accuracy from 42.0 % 42.0\% to 44.9 % 44.9\% with one CT token and 45.4 % 45.4\% with three CT tokens. These results suggest that allocating more CT can be beneficial.

sections.heading: C.2 Controlled Baseline Comparisons
sections.text: We conduct additional controlled comparisons to distinguish the benefit of implicit reasoning from two simpler explanations: removing natural-language rationales and shortening explicit reasoning traces. All experiments in this section use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct.

sections.heading: No Reasoning.
sections.text: We first consider a no reasoning control. This baseline removes natural-language rationales, while retaining the arithmetic equations used for intermediate computation. This comparison isolates whether TAC-CoT’s improvement can be explained simply by removing verbose natural-language reasoning. As shown in Table 7 , TAC-CoT improves the average accuracy from 42.0% to 45.4% in the no-tool setting.

sections.heading: Concise Explicit-CoT with Tools.
sections.text: We further compare against a concise explicit-CoT agent with the same tool-enabled setting. Specifically, we extend TokenSkip to tool use and apply the same 50% compression ratio used in our main experiments, thereby shortening explicit reasoning traces while preserving explicit reasoning and tool interaction. TAC-CoT achieves an average accuracy of 53.9%, compared with 45.4% for TokenSkip with tools. The improvement is consistent across GSM8K, GSM-Hard, and SVAMP. sections.heading: C.4 Impact of the Tool-Use Budget
sections.text: To investigate how the number of permitted tool-use affects performance, we conduct an ablation study on GSM8K samples containing four or more equations, since each equation corresponds to a potential calculator invocation. We vary the maximum number of calculator calls from 0 to 4, and also evaluate with unlimited calls. As shown in Figure 8 , accuracy improves monotonically as the number of allowed tool calls increases. This suggests that each additional tool call can contribute to mitigate error propagation during multi-step reasoning.

sections.heading: C.5 Impact of Error Accumulation
sections.text: As shown in Figure 7 , we trained GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on GSM8k-Aug and GSM8K-Aug-NL to analyze how intermediate reasoning errors accumulate as reasoning depth increases. In these datasets, equations are inserted into explicit reasoning. When gold reasoning is provided, GSM8K-Aug-NL-trained models outperform models trained on GSM8K-Aug, which are not trained to generate natural-language rationales. However, this advantage progressively diminishes as the number of generated reasoning steps increases. This trend suggests that, although explicit natural language reasoning can be beneficial under oracle reasoning conditions, error accumulation during intermediate steps can degrade accuracy. The degradation is less pronounced for the larger 1B model, which is consistent with prior observations that larger models are more robust to error accumulation in multi-step reasoning von Recum et al. sections.heading: C.6 Wall-Clock Speedup of TAC-CoT
sections.text: We additionally report wall-clock inference time on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. As shown in Table 10 , TAC-CoT consistently reduces both the number of forward passes and end-to-end latency compared with the Explicit-CoT agent. On average, TAC-CoT uses 2.3 × \times fewer forward passes on the math benchmarks and 5.5 × \times fewer forward passes on the QA benchmarks. These reductions also translate into practical wall-clock speedups: TAC-CoT runs 2.3 × \times faster on math benchmarks and 2.4 × \times faster on QA benchmarks on average. When isolating model generation time by excluding external overheads, the speedup further increases, reaching up to 3.8 × \times . These speedups are smaller than the reductions in forward passes because forward-pass count does not translate linearly into end-to-end latency. In our current implementation, total latency still includes non-optimized execution paths, parallelization overheads, and API-call latency. Thus, while TAC-CoT already provides consistent practical speedups in wall-clock time, the gap between forward-pass reduction and realized latency reduction suggests that further gains are possible with more optimized implementation and execution-level parallelization.

sections.heading: Continuous thought token injection.
sections.text: The continuous thought token c t ∈ ℝ d c_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is produced by applying a projection head Proj θ \mathrm{Proj}_{\theta} to the last hidden state of the transformer: c t = Proj θ ​ ( h t ) c_{t}=\mathrm{Proj}_{\theta}(h_{t}) , where h t h_{t} is extracted from the final layer at the last sequence position. The continuous token is fed back to the model via inputs_embeds , bypassing the vocabulary embedding lookup entirely. No vocabulary index is ever assigned to a continuous thought token.

sections.heading: Route selection and observation injection.
sections.text: At the end of each latent segment, c B c_{B} is fed via inputs_embeds to obtain route logits. If the [[ANSWER]] logit exceeds ℓ [[EXPLICIT]] \ell_{\texttt{[[EXPLICIT]]}} , the model switches to answer generation; otherwise, action tokens are generated greedily until a stop token ( </action> ). Upon a tool call, the closing action token and the returned observation text are concatenated and processed in a single forward pass, after which the latent iteration loop restarts. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8 × 6.8\times . Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding authors. (2026) ; Wei et al. (2026) . 1 Introduction To enhance the problem-solving ability of large language models (LLMs), a wide range of reasoning-oriented methods have been explored. In particular, for tasks that require accurate and reliable reasoning, such as mathematical reasoning and knowledge-intensive question answering, research has evolved toward Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning, which improves models’ internal reasoning capabilities through intermediate reasoning steps Wei et al. (2022) ; DeepSeek-AI et al. (2025b) , as well as agentic tool-use frameworks, which enhance rigor and factuality by enabling models to interact with external tools during problem solving Zhang et al. (2026) ; Kim et al. (2026) . Figure 2: Overview of TAC-CoT compared with the Explicit-CoT agent and implicit-CoT methods. TAC-CoT uses implicit CoT as its reasoning backbone while preserving interaction segments in explicit natural language. This design enables implicit CoT to use tools and allocate query-dependent implicit reasoning budgets, improving efficiency, performance, and robustness over the Explicit-CoT agent. Here, n n denotes the number of discrete tokens generated by the Explicit-CoT agent at each step, b b denotes the number of continuous tokens in each implicit reasoning segment of TAC-CoT , and m m denotes the fixed continuous-token budget used by prior implicit-CoT methods. Most prior work adopts the explicit CoT paradigm, where intermediate reasoning is represented as human-readable natural-language tokens. This paradigm is attractive because it is directly compatible with autoregressive generation and provides an interpretable interface between reasoning and action Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) . However, verbalizing the entire reasoning process substantially increases inference cost as reasoning traces grow longer and makes the model more susceptible to error accumulation across intermediate steps Han et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2026) . Implicit CoT has emerged as an alternative paradigm that replaces readable natural-language rationales with compact continuous thought tokens . By performing reasoning in non-verbal latent spaces, implicit CoT aims to retain the benefits of multi-step reasoning while mitigating the inference cost and vulnerability to error accumulation of lengthy textual traces Shen et al. (2025) . Despite these benefits, implicit CoT methods are ill-suited for LLM-based agent systems. They rely on a fixed number of implicit tokens to carry the entire reasoning process of every query, which gives rise to two limitations. First, since the implicit-token budget is consumed in a single uninterrupted block before the final answer Deng et al. (2024) ; Wei et al. (2026) , there is no intermediate point at which the model can emit an explicit tool call or ingest an observation, so tool use is structurally infeasible. Second, the same token count is applied to every input regardless of its difficulty or the number of intermediate decision points it requires Wu et al. (2026) ; Aggarwal et al. (2026) . As a result, prior implicit CoT methods cannot interact with external environments and under-allocate reasoning capacity to more difficult queries. In this paper, we propose TAC-CoT ( T ool-empowered A daptive C ontinuous CoT), which interleaves compact implicit reasoning segments with explicit tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers . Rather than carrying the entire reasoning process in a single block of implicit tokens, TAC-CoT reasons within a short implicit segment and then either invokes a tool or produces the answer, resuming with another segment after each tool observation. This interleaving simultaneously addresses both limitations of prior implicit CoT, as explicit tokens between segments make tool use executable, while the number of segments, determined on the fly, makes the reasoning budget query-adaptive. To train this behavior, we automatically construct tool-use trajectories from reasoning datasets and supervise the model to perform compact latent reasoning between tool invocations. Our contributions are summarized as follows. (1) We extend implicit CoT to tool-empowered agentic systems, enabling compact continuous reasoning in iterative reasoning–action workflows. (2) We show that TAC-CoT improves reasoning performance while substantially reducing the number of reasoning tokens compared with explicit CoT-style reasoning by interleaving continuous thought tokens with explicit tokens. (3) We introduce an adaptive token-allocation mechanism that flexibly adjusts the length of implicit reasoning according to query difficulty. (4) As highlighted in Figure 1 , TAC-CoT improves downstream task performance while using the forward reasoning budget more efficiently. Our analysis shows that TAC-CoT benefits from query-adaptive implicit reasoning budgets, improves tool-using scenarios, and mitigates error accumulation through implicit reasoning. 2 TAC-CoT : Tool-Empowered Implicit CoT via Interleaving Explicit Tokens We explain TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered implicit CoT framework that interleaves latent reasoning segments with explicit, executable tool interactions. We first describe TAC-CoT ’s inference procedure (§ 2.1 ), then how we construct training trajectories (§ 2.2 ), and finally the learning objective (§ 2.3 ). Algorithm 1 shows its inference procedure. 2.1 Tool-Interleaved Implicit CoT with Query-Adaptive Budgets The key idea of TAC-CoT is to jointly leverage implicit reasoning tokens and textual tokens for tool-use trajectories. In this process, the length of the reasoning tokens is adaptively adjusted according to the query. As shown in Figure 2 , this produces an interleaved trajectory that preserves the executable interface of tool-using agents without verbalizing every intermediate step. A key design decision of TAC-CoT is when to interrupt latent reasoning for an external interaction. At the end of every implicit segment C ( i ) C^{(i)} , TAC-CoT compares the logits of the tool call u ( i ) u^{(i)} and answer options to decide the next step. If the tool-call logit is higher, TAC-CoT emits a tool call, appends the returned observation o ( i ) o^{(i)} to the context, and starts another implicit segment. Otherwise, the current segment becomes the consolidating segment C ( k ) C^{(k)} , from which the final answer is generated. Unlike prior implicit CoT methods that consume a fixed implicit budget before any explicit output, this per-segment routing is what makes tool use feasible under implicit reasoning. Query-Adaptive Continuous-Thought Token Budget. Since the tool call decision is made after every implicit segment, the total reasoning budget becomes query-adaptive . Simple queries may terminate after a single segment, while more complex queries can continue through multiple tool interactions. Thus, b b is fixed only locally within each segment. That is, each example must provide the full sequence of explicit reasoning segments ℛ ( i ) \mathcal{R}^{(i)} , tool calls u ( i ) u^{(i)} , observations o ( i ) o^{(i)} , and the final answer a a , from which TAC-CoT learns to replace each ℛ ( i ) \mathcal{R}^{(i)} with an implicit segment C ( i ) C^{(i)} while preserving the surrounding explicit interactions. We construct such data with two strategies depending on whether the source dataset already includes executable tool interactions, or only reasoning traces and gold answers. • Sources with Tool Interactions. We convert the provided executable annotations into tool calls. If the executable annotations are provided separately from the reasoning traces, we match their tool-call parameters and returned observations to the corresponding reasoning spans. We then normalize the matched interactions into a unified tool-call format with explicit tool names and parameters, and insert the tool calls and observations into the reasoning trajectory. • Sources without Tool Interactions. As intermediate interactions are not directly available, we instead employ a stronger LLM (DeepSeek-V3; See Appendix A ) as a tool-augmented solver to synthesize them. Given a question and the available tools, the model generates a complete trajectory with interleaved reasoning spans, tool calls, observations, and a predicted answer. TAC-CoT requires training to use implicit tokens. To evaluate mathematical reasoning, we use GSM8K-Aug-NL ( Deng et al., 2024 ) , which contains explicit interactions as textual explanations. Since GSM8K-Aug-NL contains explicit reasoning trajectories without executable interfaces, we insert executable calculator annotations from GSM8K-Aug ( Deng et al., 2024 ) . To evaluate QA capability, we use the HotpotQA Yang et al. (2018) dataset. We construct 40,000 trajectories by using DeepSeek-V3 ( DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025a ) with the available tool and allowing it to solve each question through iterative tool interaction. We retain only trajectories whose final answer matches the gold annotation. Although teacher-generated trajectories may inherit teacher-specific biases, TAC-CoT and all QA baselines are trained on the same trajectories; such biases are therefore shared across methods and cannot by themselves explain TAC-CoT’s relative improvements. Dataset construction details are provided in Appendix A . Evaluation Benchmarks. We evaluate TAC-CoT on agentic math problem solving (Math), agentic Question-Answering (QA), and tool-use benchmarks, as summarized in Table 1 . On toolBench, we use ‘Single’ for the I1 single-tool scenario, and ‘Multi’ as the I2 + I3 multi-tool scenario. We report accuracy (Acc) for math tasks and exact match (EM) for QA. To compare the inference cost independently of hardware and external API latency , we report the average number of forward passes (# Fwd) Kuzina et al. (2026) ; Wei et al. (2026) . For no-tool QA setting (TU = ✗ ), # Fwd also includes autoregressive generation of missing tool observations; see Appendix B.2 . Implementation Details. We use Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) , and Qwen3-4B Yang et al. (2025) as backbone models. For agentic QA, we use the Wikipedia API as the search engine, following Yao et al. (2022) . Further details are provided in Appendix B . We provide pseudocode for reproducibility in Figure 10 . For TAC-CoT , we set B = 3 B=3 . Ablation results for different B B values are provided in Appendix C.1 . Baselines. We compare TAC-CoT against (1) an Explicit-CoT agent, which serves as a strong baseline for tool use and reasoning by using full explicit reasoning traces, fine-tuned on the same training trajectories as our method; (2) TokenSkip Xia et al. (2025) , an explicit CoT method that compresses intermediate reasoning trajectories by pruning low-importance tokens; (3) PCCoT Wu et al. (2025) , which updates implicit thought tokens in parallel using Jacobi iteration, improving efficiency over sequential implicit CoT; (4) CODI Shen et al. (2025) , an implicit-CoT method trained via trajectory-level self-distillation from CoT-based teacher signals; and (5) SIM-CoT Wei et al. (2026) , which extends CODI by adding step-level supervision to reconstruct reasoning steps from latent embeddings. 3.2 Main Results Our evaluation examines whether TAC-CoT achieves its design goals in addressing the limitations of extending existing CoT approaches to agentic systems, focusing on four aspects: tool-use effectiveness, internal reasoning ability, query-adaptive continuous-thought budgeting, and inference efficiency. Table 2 presents the main results on agentic math and QA benchmarks across tool-calling and no-tool settings. Performance on Agentic Reasoning. Overall, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms Explicit-CoT and the other baselines. Averaged over all backbone models, Our method improves math accuracy by 5.8%p and QA performance by 2.4 points compared with Explicit-CoT. The gains also transfer to out-of-domain benchmarks: Ours improves math performance by 6.5%p in-domain and 5.5%p out-of-domain, and QA performance by 2.4 points in-domain and 2.5 points out-of-domain. This consistent trend suggests that TAC-CoT provides robust adaptive implicit reasoning beyond the training-domain distribution. To isolate the effect of implicit reasoning from external tool execution, we compare TAC-CoT with other baselines in the no-tool setting on math datasets. While TokenSkip, which shortens rationales by pruning tokens, underperforms Explicit-CoT, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms the Explicit-CoT agent across all math datasets. These results indicate that the improvement in internal reasoning does not simply come from shorter reasoning traces. Consistently, TAC-CoT also outperforms baselines that either remove natural-language reasoning entirely or retain concise, explicit reasoning with tool use; see Appendix C.2 . Effectiveness of TAC-CoT . The effectiveness of TAC-CoT comes from both tool-use and query-adaptive implicit reasoning. Tool-use substantially improves QA performance, yielding up to a 29.9 point average gain over the no-tool variant while reducing forward passes by 13.3 × \times on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Even without tools, TAC-CoT benefits from adaptive budgeting: on math benchmarks, its no-tool variant outperforms prior implicit-CoT baselines while requiring far fewer forward passes than explicit CoT. These results show that TAC-CoT improves efficiency and performance by adaptively allocating continuous reasoning, with additional gains when external knowledge is needed. Query-Adaptive Continuous-Thought Budget. Unlike prior implicit-CoT methods that use a fixed continuous-token budget for every query, TAC-CoT adaptively allocates its total reasoning budget according to the query. This query-adaptive continuous-thought budgeting contributes to the performance gains, especially for math tasks that depend on internal reasoning. As shown in Figure 6 , the benefit becomes larger as the required number of reasoning steps increases. TAC-CoT ’s query-adaptive budgeting benefits inputs that require different amounts of internal deliberation before producing the final answer. We group GSM8K examples into five subsets according to the number of gold reasoning steps, ranging from one to five steps, and treat this number as the required reasoning depth. We then evaluate each subset separately and compare TAC-CoT without tool use against SIM-CoT, a state-of-the-art fixed-budget implicit-CoT baseline, using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. Figure 6 shows that TAC-CoT consistently outperforms SIM-CoT across all reasoning-depth groups, with larger gains on examples that require more reasoning steps. The improvement increases from 4.6 points on one-step examples to 30.3 points on four-step examples. This trend suggests that assigning the same continuous-thought-token budget to every input becomes increasingly restrictive as the required number of reasoning steps grows. In contrast, TAC-CoT increases the total continuous-token budget by continuing through additional implicit reasoning segments when more reasoning steps are needed. These results demonstrate that TAC-CoT flexibly allocates reasoning budget across queries, which is especially important for reasoning-intensive tasks. Inference Efficiency. TAC-CoT substantially reduces inference cost relative to Explicit-CoT while improving task accuracy. Across backbones, it reduces the per-query forward count by up to 2.6 × 2.6\times on math benchmarks and 6.8 × 6.8\times on QA benchmarks, with larger savings on QA due to longer multi-step trajectories. This suggests that TAC-CoT becomes increasingly beneficial for longer trajectories. Although fixed-budget implicit-CoT baselines use fewer forward passes, they do not adapt to query complexity or retrieve missing observations. This limitation is especially harmful for QA, where answers often depend on retrieved evidence, leading to pronounced performance degradation. In contrast, TAC-CoT achieves a better cost–performance trade-off by reducing inference cost relative to Explicit-CoT while avoiding the QA degradation of fixed-budget implicit-CoT methods. On a single NVIDIA L40S GPU, TAC-CoT achieves measured wall-clock speedups of 2.3× on math and 2.4× on QA. Since realized latency depends on hardware, implementation, and external API overhead, #Fwd reductions should not be interpreted directly as wall-clock speedups; see Appendix C.6 for full results. 4 Related Works Explicit and Implicit CoT. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improves the reasoning ability of large language models by generating intermediate reasoning before the final answer Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) . CoT methods are commonly categorized as explicit or implicit, depending on whether intermediate reasoning is represented as discrete tokens or continuous representations. Explicit CoT is readable and easy to supervise Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) , but decoding long reasoning traces increases inference cost Han et al. (2025) ; Xia et al. (2025) and exacerbates stepwise error accumulation Wu et al. (2026) . Implicit CoT instead performs intermediate reasoning in continuous latent space Hao et al. (2025) ; Shen et al. (2025) ; Wu et al. (2025) ; Wei et al. (2026) ; Kuzina et al. (2026) . For example, Coconut feeds hidden states back as continuous thought tokens Hao et al. (2025) , CODI distills explicit CoT into continuous representations Shen et al. (2025) , PCCoT updates latent thought tokens in parallel for efficient inference Wu et al. (2025) , and SIM-CoT stabilizes implicit reasoning via step-level reconstruction Wei et al. (2026) . Although these methods reduce the cost of verbalized reasoning, they are mainly designed for standalone reasoning: they typically allocate a fixed number of continuous thought tokens per query and do not expose intermediate decisions as executable interfaces, limiting their suitability for agentic settings that require repeated reasoning and acting. In contrast, TAC-CoT extends implicit CoT to tool-using agentic systems by interleaving compact latent reasoning segments with explicit tool interactions, enabling tool calling and query-adaptive reasoning budgets. At the same time, compared with explicit-CoT agents, TAC-CoT avoids the need to verbalize intermediate reasoning, thereby reducing inference cost and mitigating error accumulation from lengthy reasoning traces. Tool-Using LLM Agents. LLMs are increasingly studied as agents that solve tasks through interleaved reasoning, tool calls, and observations Yao et al. (2022) ; Schick et al. (2023) ; Shinn et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . ReAct formalizes this reasoning–acting loop Yao et al. (2022) , while Toolformer Schick et al. (2023) and ART Paranjape et al. (2023) show that models can invoke external APIs and resume generation after tool execution. However, most tool-using agents still rely on explicit CoT Wei et al. (2022) ; Kojima et al. (2022) ; Yao et al. (2023) , whose repeated generation across multi-step interaction loops makes inference costly Han et al. (2025) ; Xia et al. (2025) ; Aytes et al. (2025) and vulnerable to error accumulation Wu et al. (2026) . 5 Conclusion We presented TAC-CoT , a tool-empowered adaptive continuous CoT framework that extends implicit reasoning to tool-using agentic problem solving. By interleaving compact continuous reasoning segments with explicit tokens for tool calls, observations, and final answers, TAC-CoT preserves the executable interface required for agentic workflows while avoiding the cost of fully verbalized reasoning traces. Across agentic math and knowledge-intensive QA benchmarks, TAC-CoT consistently outperforms Explicit-CoT agents in both in-domain and out-of-domain settings, while using substantially fewer model forward passes. Further analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use decisions, performs better in multi-tool scenarios, mitigates error accumulation, and benefits from query-adaptive continuous thought-token allocation. Limitations This work has a few limitations: First, the adaptive routing mechanism operates at the segment level rather than the token level. Second, longer interaction horizons remain an important direction for evaluating the practical deployment of TAC-CoT . Appendix A Details of Data Construction This section provides the details of the recipe described in Section 2.2 for each domain. Math Problem Solving. The math domain follows the source-obtainable interaction setting described. For GSM8K, where data with explicit interactions already exist, we use GSM8K-Aug and GSM8K-Aug-NL, two GSM8K augmentations with 385k samples each Deng et al. (2024) . GSM8K-Aug retains only the arithmetic equations in each reasoning step (e.g., <<86.7*15*.01=13.005>> ), whereas GSM8K-Aug-NL contains only explicit reasoning (e.g. ...day, 86.7 x 15% = 13.005 coins... ). Because the two datasets have the same questions, we align examples by question and insert the equations from GSM8K-Aug into the corresponding natural language reasoning trajectory from GSM8K-Aug-NL. Question-Answering. For HotpotQA, which provides only questions and their gold answers without faithful tool-use trajectories, we construct trajectories by prompting DeepSeek-V3 to solve each question with access to a retrieval tool. Following Yao et al. (2022) , we implement a Wikipedia retrieval system and use the ReAct-style few-shot demonstrations from their setup. The prompt template is shown in Figures 11 and 12 . Quality Audit and Construction Cost. To assess the quality of the synthesized QA trajectories, we randomly sampled 200 trajectories and evaluated them using GPT-5.1, a model different from the DeepSeek-V3 teacher. The evaluator assessed whether the generated actions and final answers were logically valid, and judged 99% of the sampled trajectories to be valid. Generating the QA trajectories cost $102.73 in total, including generations discarded during answer-based filtering. The filtering pass rate was 56.24%. Because exact-match filtering may reject semantically correct answers expressed differently from the gold annotation, this procedure may underestimate the usable trajectory yield. C.6 Wall-Clock Speedup of TAC-CoT We additionally report wall-clock inference time on a single NVIDIA L40S GPU using Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. As shown in Table 10 , TAC-CoT consistently reduces both the number of forward passes and end-to-end latency compared with the Explicit-CoT agent. On average, TAC-CoT uses 2.3 × \times fewer forward passes on the math benchmarks and 5.5 × \times fewer forward passes on the QA benchmarks. These reductions also translate into practical wall-clock speedups: TAC-CoT runs 2.3 × \times faster on math benchmarks and 2.4 × \times faster on QA benchmarks on average. When isolating model generation time by excluding external overheads, the speedup further increases, reaching up to 3.8 × \times . These speedups are smaller than the reductions in forward passes because forward-pass count does not translate linearly into end-to-end latency. In our current implementation, total latency still includes non-optimized execution paths, parallelization overheads, and API-call latency. Thus, while TAC-CoT already provides consistent practical speedups in wall-clock time, the gap between forward-pass reduction and realized latency reduction suggests that further gains are possible with more optimized implementation and execution-level parallelization.
